## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered} -->

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
The earth would explode if hit by an earthquake of magnitude 18 (xkcd!)
:::

When measuring the intensity of earthquake, the metric is Richter. Moment Magnitude
One of the strongest earthquakes in Madagascar was 6.2 in 1950, 11 May (earthquakelist.org)
The strongest earthquake measured measured with a Magnitude 9.5 in 1960 Great Chilean earthquake.
According to wikipedia, 6-6.9 is strong whereas, 9-9.9 is extreme near total dectruction.
Why going from 6-10 is such a big deal.
It is because the scale is on a logarithm scale.
Concretely, if an earthquake of 6 release x energy, the 9 releases 10^ 9- 6 = 10^3 that is 10^3 = 1000 more renergy, in other words, instead of throughing one grenade, you are actually throwing one thousand!!!

The importance of log scale is to transform multiplication to addition, log(a b) = log a + log b. or above log(10^3) = log(10 * 10 *10) = log 10 + log 10 + log 10 = 3 log 10.


One might then ask if it ends at 10.
What would a say an earthquake of 12, 15, or 18?
According to xkcd, the latter will case the earth to explode.
Most of us would think that 6 to 12 is double and g to 18 will triple.
The number indeed but the energy contained is increased by 10^12

This is where it is important to realize that Richter is on base 10 a logarithmic scale.
Adding one unit, will multiply the energy by 10.
So to put it in other world. a 6 vs 9 earthquake means the latter is 1000 more powerful than the former.

The logarithm is another function but it has two main properties:
- Turns multiplication to addition:
$\log(a \times b) = \log(a) + \log(b)$ and so $\log(a^2) = \log(a \times a) = \log(a) + \log(a) = 2 \times log(a)$.

- Reciprocal of the exponential.

Why does it have those properties, let's just say it is the miracle/genuis of mathematicians who discovered it.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
A logarithm is function defined from (0, + inf) to (- inf, + inf). And is written log or ln.

The actual definition is that it is the area under the curve for 1/x.
Essentially, if you so that the area under the curve is 1.

This leads to the fancy property, that is log(e) = 1.
And this implies that log(e^x) = x log e = x.
In other words, log is the reciprocal of exponential.

Logarithm and bases
log2 = ln/log2, and log10 = ln/log10


Here are the standard formal definitions found in foundational mathematical analysis and calculus textbooks.

1. The Inverse Function Definition
This definition builds the logarithm directly on top of the pre-established formal definition of an exponential function.

Textbook Source
Book: Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd Edition, 1976)
Author: Walter Rudin
SCIRP
Publisher: McGraw-Hill
SCIRP

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 8 ("Some Special Functions"), after establishing that the exponential function exp(x) is continuous, strictly increasing, and maps the real line R bijectively onto the positive real numbers (0,∞), Rudin defines its inverse:
"The logarithmic function log is defined as the inverse of the exponential function. That is, for every y>0, x=log(y) is the unique real number such that:
$\exp(x) = y$


```{r}
x <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.0001)
y <- exp(x)

par(pty = "s")
plot(x, y,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "x",
     ylab = "y",
     ylim = c(-4, 4),
     xlim = c(-4, 4),
     xaxs = "i",
     yaxs = "i",
     asp = 1,
     main = "",
     las = 1)
# Add natural logarithm
lines(x[x > 0], log(x[x > 0]), col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Add identity line (y = x)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# Add legend
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("exp(x)", "ln(x)", "y = x"),
       col = c("black", "red", "blue"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       lwd = 2)

```


- For an arbitrary base a>0 (a!=1), the general logarithm function loga(y) is defined via the same inverse relationship to the base-a exponential function:
Britannica
$x = \log_a(y) \iff a^x = y$

$\log_a x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a} \quad \text{for } x > 0, \, a > 0, \, a \neq 1$


## Examples {.unnumbered}


- $\log(1) = 0$ where it intersect with x.

- $\log(e) = 1$ by definition.

- For $0 < x < 1$, $\log(1/x) = \log(x-1) = - 1 \times \log(x) = - \log(x)$ hence $\log (x)$ is always negative.

- $\log(n!) = \log(1 \times 2 \times 3 \times \cdots \times n) =  \log (1) + \log (2) + \cdots + \log(n) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \log(i)$

- $\log(\exp{- \frac{x^2}{2}}) = - \frac{x^2}{2}$

- Linearization of a power-law i.e. of the form f(x) = c x^z
  - Species-area relationship S = c A^z, on a log scale
  - Metabolic scaling

- Salary

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}

- By definition cannot take negative number and is not defined at 0
- [Semantic: $\ln$ and $\log$]{.highlight-semantic}.

- Used in likelihood to turn a product into sum.

- Transforming  0 to something, shift to log(x + 1)

- Integral defintion: For every x>0, we define the natural logarithm of x, denoted by $\ln(x)$, by the formula:
$\ln x = \int_{1}^{x} \frac{1}{t} \, dt$

- Two ways of visualization. Classical just transforming the y-axis, or taking the log and plotting normally


```{r}
# 1. Dataset setup
df_vals <- data.frame(
  category = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  value = c(60, 500, 2500, 5000)
)

# Compute log10 values for explicit transformation
df_vals$log10_val <- log10(df_vals$value)

# 2. Set up side-by-side layout (1 row, 2 columns) with top margin for labels
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 4, 2))

# ==============================================================================
# LEFT PANEL: Native Log Scale (log = "y")
# ==============================================================================
bp1 <- barplot(
  height = df_vals$value,
  names.arg = df_vals$category,
  main = "Native Log Scale (log = 'y')",
  ylab = "Value (Log Scale)",
  col = "#1f77b4", border = NA,
  log = "y",
  ylim = c(1, max(df_vals$value) * 3),
  las = 1
)


# Redraw bars over grid without repeating y-axis ticks
barplot(df_vals$value, add = TRUE, col = "#1f77b4", border = NA, log = "y", yaxt = "n", ann = FALSE)

# Value labels above bars (Raw numbers)
text(
  x = bp1, y = df_vals$value,
  labels = format(df_vals$value, big.mark = ","),
  pos = 3, cex = 0.85, col = "#333333", font = 2, xpd = TRUE
)

grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# ==============================================================================
# RIGHT PANEL: Converted log10 Values
# ==============================================================================
bp2 <- barplot(
  height = df_vals$log10_val,
  names.arg = df_vals$category,
  main = expression(paste("Transformed Values (", log[10], "(y))")),
  ylab = expression(paste(log[10], "(Value)")),
  col = "#2ca02c", border = NA,
  ylim = c(0, max(df_vals$log10_val) * 1.15),
  las = 1
)


# Redraw bars over grid without repeating y-axis ticks
barplot(df_vals$log10_val, add = TRUE, col = "#2ca02c", border = NA, yaxt = "n", ann = FALSE)

# Value labels above bars (log10 numbers rounded to 2 decimal places)
text(
  x = bp2, y = df_vals$log10_val,
  labels = round(df_vals$log10_val, 2),
  pos = 3, cex = 0.85, col = "#333333", font = 2, xpd = TRUE
)
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Reset plotting parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```


- Salary


```{r}
# 1. Data frame setup
df_salary <- data.frame(
  job = factor(
    c("Intern", "Technician", "Senior Employee", "Team leader", "Supervisor",
      "Manager", "Director", "Vice-president", "Chief Officer", "CEO"),
    levels = c("Intern", "Technician", "Senior Employee", "Team leader", "Supervisor",
               "Manager", "Director", "Vice-president", "Chief Officer", "CEO")
  ),
  salary = c(2, 4, 6, 12, 50, 100, 250, 600, 2000, 5000) # values in ten thousands
)

# 2. Set up side-by-side layout with bottom margin for rotated labels
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(8, 5, 4, 2))

# ==============================================================================
# LEFT PANEL: Linear Scale
# ==============================================================================
bp1 <- barplot(
  height = df_salary$salary,
  names.arg = FALSE,
  main = "Linear Scale",
  ylab = "Salary",
  col = "#1f77b4", border = NA,
  ylim = c(0, max(df_salary$salary) * 1.15),
  las = 1
)

grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Redraw bars over grid (yaxt = "n" prevents duplicated y-axis ticks)
barplot(df_salary$salary, add = TRUE, col = "#1f77b4", border = NA, yaxt = "n", ann = FALSE)

# Custom rotated x-axis labels
text(x = bp1, y = -max(df_salary$salary) * 0.04, labels = df_salary$job,
     srt = 45, adj = 1, xpd = TRUE, cex = 0.8)

## Raw numerical value labels above bars
#text(x = bp1, y = df_salary$salary, labels = format(df_salary$salary, big.mark = ","),
#     pos = 3, cex = 0.65, col = "#333333", xpd = TRUE)


# ==============================================================================
# RIGHT PANEL: Logarithmic Scale
# ==============================================================================
bp2 <- barplot(
  height = df_salary$salary,
  names.arg = FALSE,
  main = "Logarithmic Scale (log10)",
  ylab = "Salary (Log Scale)",
  col = "#2ca02c", border = NA,
  log = "y",
  ylim = c(1, max(df_salary$salary) * 3),
  las = 1
)

grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Redraw bars over grid without repeating axis text
barplot(df_salary$salary, add = TRUE, col = "#2ca02c", border = NA, log = "y", yaxt = "n", ann = FALSE)

# Custom rotated x-axis labels (positioned relative to log axis baseline)
text(x = bp2, y = 0.6, labels = df_salary$job,
     srt = 45, adj = 1, xpd = TRUE, cex = 0.8)

## Raw numerical value labels above bars
#text(x = bp2, y = df_salary$salary, labels = format(df_salary$salary, big.mark = ","),
#     pos = 3, cex = 0.65, col = "#333333", xpd = TRUE)

# Reset plotting parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

- Convergence: is the temperature at equilibrium?


```{r}
# 1. Define power law function: f(x) = 1 + 10 / x^1.5
f <- function(x) 1 + 10 / (x^1.5)

# Setup x domains
x_lin <- seq(1, 1000, length.out = 1000)
x_log <- 10^seq(0, 3, length.out = 1000) # log-spaced vector from 10^0 to 10^3

# Colors
curve_col <- "#1f77b4"
limit_col <- "#d62728"

# 2. Set up side-by-side layout (1 row, 2 columns)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 2))

# ==============================================================================
# LEFT PANEL: Linear Scale (Appears Almost Converged)
# ==============================================================================
plot(x_lin, f(x_lin), type = "l", col = curve_col, lwd = 2.5,
     xlim = c(1, 1000), ylim = c(0.8, 11), las = 1,
     main = "Linear Scale (Looks Converged)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)")

grid(col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")
abline(h = 1, col = limit_col, lty = 2, lwd = 1.8)

# Highlight points
pts_x <- c(1, 10, 100, 1000)
pts_y <- f(pts_x)
points(pts_x, pts_y, col = curve_col, pch = 19, cex = 1.2)

# Annotation for linear convergence illusion
text(500, 1.3, labels = "Appears flat & converged near y = 1",
     col = curve_col, pos = 3, font = 2, cex = 0.85)
text(800, 1.0, labels = "Asymptote y = 1", col = limit_col, pos = 3, cex = 0.8)


# ==============================================================================
# RIGHT PANEL: Logarithmic Scale (Reveals Ongoing Heavy-Tail Decay)
# ==============================================================================
plot(x_log, f(x_log), type = "l", col = curve_col, lwd = 2.5,
     log = "x", xlim = c(1, 1000), ylim = c(0.8, 11), las = 1,
     main = "Logarithmic Scale (Reveals Slow Tail)",
     xlab = "x (Log Scale)", ylab = "f(x)")

grid(col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")
abline(h = 1, col = limit_col, lty = 2, lwd = 1.8)

# Highlight and label exact points on log scale
points(pts_x, pts_y, col = curve_col, pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
text(pts_x, pts_y, labels = paste0(" f(", pts_x, ") = ", round(pts_y, 3)),
     pos = c(4, 4, 3, 3), cex = 0.8, col = "#333333", font = 2)

text(10, 1.0, labels = "Asymptote y = 1", col = limit_col, pos = 1, cex = 0.8)

# Reset layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

- Data from species area relationship


```{r}
# 1. Dataset: Sunda Islands Land Birds (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967)
sunda_data <- data.frame(
  island = c("Christmas", "Enggano", "Bangka", "Bali", "Lombok",
             "Sumba", "Flores", "Sumbawa", "Celebes (Sulawesi)", "Java", "Sumatra", "Borneo"),
  area_sq_mi = c(60, 160, 4370, 2095, 1820,
                 4300, 5850, 5960, 72000, 48800, 182000, 287000),
  species = c(15, 32, 119, 133, 118,
              112, 138, 132, 257, 340, 375, 420)
)

# Fit log10 linear model to derive power law parameters (S = c * A^z)
fit <- lm(log10(species) ~ log10(area_sq_mi), data = sunda_data)
z     <- coef(fit)[2]          # Slope (z ~ 0.28)
c_val <- 10^(coef(fit)[1])     # Constant c (~ 4.8)

# Smooth evaluation domain for linear curve fitting
a_seq <- 10^seq(1.5, 5.6, length.out = 500)
s_fit <- c_val * (a_seq^z)

# Setup 2-panel layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 2))

# ==============================================================================
# LEFT PANEL: Normal (Linear) Scale
# ==============================================================================
plot(sunda_data$area_sq_mi, sunda_data$species,
     xlim = c(0, 300000), ylim = c(0, 450), las = 1,
     xlab = expression(paste("Island Area (mi"^2, ")")),
     ylab = "Number of Bird Species (S)",
     main = "Linear Scale (S = cA^z)",
     col = "#1f77b4", pch = 19, cex = 1.3)

grid(col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Draw fitted power-law curve
lines(a_seq, s_fit, col = "#d62728", lwd = 2)

# Redraw points over grid
points(sunda_data$area_sq_mi, sunda_data$species, col = "#1f77b4", pch = 19, cex = 1.3)

# Label key extreme islands (small islands crushed near origin; large islands at right)
text(sunda_data$area_sq_mi[sunda_data$island %in% c("Borneo", "Sumatra", "Java", "Celebes (Sulawesi)")],
     sunda_data$species[sunda_data$island %in% c("Borneo", "Sumatra", "Java", "Celebes (Sulawesi)")],
     labels = sunda_data$island[sunda_data$island %in% c("Borneo", "Sumatra", "Java", "Celebes (Sulawesi)")],
     pos = 2, cex = 0.75, col = "#333333")


# ==============================================================================
# RIGHT PANEL: Log-Log Scale
# ==============================================================================
plot(sunda_data$area_sq_mi, sunda_data$species,
     log = "xy", las = 1,
     xlim = c(40, 400000), ylim = c(10, 500),
     xlab = expression(paste("Island Area (mi"^2, " - Log Scale)")),
     ylab = "Number of Bird Species (S - Log Scale)",
     main = expression(paste("Log-Log Scale (log S = log c + z log A)")),
     col = "#1f77b4", pch = 19, cex = 1.3)

grid(col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Draw linearized regression line
abline(fit, col = "#d62728", lwd = 2)

# Redraw points over grid
points(sunda_data$area_sq_mi, sunda_data$species, col = "#1f77b4", pch = 19, cex = 1.3)

# Label islands on log scale
text(sunda_data$area_sq_mi, sunda_data$species,
     labels = sunda_data$island, pos = 4, cex = 0.7, col = "#333333", xpd = TRUE)

# Annotate fitted power law parameters
legend("topleft",
       legend = c(paste0("Slope (z) = ", round(z, 2)),
                  paste0("c = ", round(c_val, 2)),
                  paste0("R\u00b2 = ", round(summary(fit)$r.squared, 2))),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85, text.col = "#d62728")

# Reset layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

<!--
1. The Integral Definition (The Analytic Approach)
In rigorous calculus courses, defining the logarithm as an inverse can lead to circular logic if the exponential function wasn't constructed cleanly. To avoid this, advanced textbooks define the natural logarithm (lnx) from scratch as the area under a hyperbola.

Textbook Source
Book: Calculus (Volume 1, 2nd Edition, 1967)
Author: Tom M. Apostol
Publisher: John Wiley & Sons

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 6 ("The Logarithm, the Exponential, and the Inverse Trigonometric Functions"), Apostol defines the natural logarithm function for any positive real number x using a Riemann integral:
"For every x>0, we define the natural logarithm of x, denoted by lnx, by the formula:
$\ln x = \int_{1}^{x} \frac{1}{t} \, dt$
"
From this fundamental calculus definition, all algebraic properties of logarithms are derived as theorems. For example, the product rule ln(ab)=lna+lnb is proven strictly using the additive properties of definite integrals.

3. Generalization to Any Base via the Integral Definition
Once the natural logarithm (lnx) is established analytically via the integral method above, the general logarithm function for any valid base a is formally defined using the change-of-base formula: -->
